Green Computing Infrastructure

THE CORE IDEA
Greener computing is about smarter choices
Choose cleaner windows
Reduce carbon by choosing cleaner times and places to run work.
Match real demand
Match computing power and active hardware to real demand.
02

TECHNIQUE 01
Carbon-aware scheduling shifts flexible work
01
Check the signal
Check carbon intensity by time and location.
02
Move the work
Move a non-urgent workload to a cleaner window.
03
Run with less carbon
Run the same computation with potentially lower emissions.
Example: an ML training job that takes four hours can run later if its deadline allows.
03

TECHNIQUE 02
DVFS uses only the performance a task needs
Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling adjusts processor voltage and frequency to workload.
1
Heavy AI processing
Needs more performance.
2
Processor setting

3

Lower voltage and frequency can reduce power when full speed is unnecessary.

FROM PRINCIPLE TO PRACTICE
Real-World Case Studies
Each example matches demand to cleaner timing, lighter processing, or fewer active machines.
Carbon-aware scheduling
Google’s carbon-intelligent computing shifts flexible compute toward lower-carbon times and locations; demand response can move non-urgent video processing and translation work.
Google Cloud Blog · Google-authored research
DVFS on smartphones
A phone can use higher processor performance for gaming, then lower voltage and frequency while you read a message.
Supplied notes
Energy-proportional data centers
At night, a cloud data center can consolidate workloads onto fewer servers and place unused resources in low-power states.

THE SYSTEM VIEW
Five techniques, one operating principle
Technique | Main decision | Potential benefit
Carbon-aware scheduling | When or where to run | Cleaner electricity window
DVFS | How fast the processor should run | Less power for lighter work
Energy-proportional computing | How much infrastructure stays active | Less idle energy
VM scheduling | Where virtual machines run | Fewer active servers
Container scheduling | Where and when containers run | Higher utilization
09

TECHNIQUE 01
Edge–Cloud Collaborative Computing
Distributes computing tasks between nearby edge devices and centralized cloud data centers to improve efficiency and reduce energy consumption.
HOW IT WORKS
01
Edge computing
Processes data near its source, such as IoT devices or local servers.
02
Cloud computing
Handles complex computations, large-scale storage and intensive analytics.
03
Collaboration
Assigns each task to edge or cloud based on processing needs, latency and energy use.
Green Computing Techniques
02
Notes: Edge–cloud collaborative computing splits work between edge devices near the data source and centralized cloud data centers. The edge handles quick, local processing; the cloud handles heavy computation, storage and analytics. Tasks are assigned based on processing requirements, latency and energy usage.

TECHNIQUE 01 · IN PRACTICE
Process locally, send only what matters
GREEN COMPUTING TECHNIQUES
Process time-sensitive data locally to reduce data transmission.
Send only necessary data to the cloud.
Allocate workloads to energy-efficient computing resources.
Reduce network traffic and unnecessary cloud processing.
EXAMPLE · SMART CAMPUS
Classroom sensors process temperature and occupancy data locally, while the cloud analyzes long-term energy consumption patterns.
BENEFITS
Lower energy use
Less network traffic
Faster response
Better resource use
Green Computing Techniques
03
Notes: Green techniques: process time-sensitive data locally, send only necessary data to the cloud, allocate workloads to energy-efficient resources, and reduce network traffic. Example: in a smart campus, classroom sensors handle temperature and occupancy locally while the cloud studies long-term energy patterns. Benefits: lower energy consumption, reduced network traffic, faster response and improved resource utilization.

TECHNIQUE 02
Thermal-Aware Data Center Optimization
Manages server workloads, cooling systems and airflow based on temperature conditions to reduce energy consumption and prevent overheating.
HOW IT WORKS
01
Temperature monitoring
Sensors continuously track server and rack temperatures.
02
Heat analysis
Identifies hot spots and areas with inefficient cooling.
03
Workload scheduling
Moves tasks to servers with suitable thermal conditions.
04
Cooling optimization
Adjusts fans, airflow and cooling to actual requirements.
Green Computing Techniques
04
Notes: Thermal-aware optimization uses temperature data to manage workloads, cooling and airflow. Sensors monitor server and rack temperatures, heat analysis finds hot spots, workloads move to servers with suitable thermal conditions, and cooling is adjusted to what is actually needed.

TECHNIQUE 02 · IN PRACTICE
Cool what's hot, not the whole room
GREEN COMPUTING TECHNIQUES
Use intelligent cooling systems.
Apply temperature-based workload allocation.
Improve hot-aisle and cold-aisle separation.
Avoid unnecessary cooling and excessive fan operation.
EXAMPLE · HOT SERVER RACK
When one rack becomes too hot, some workloads shift to cooler servers, reducing overheating and improving cooling efficiency.
BENEFITS
Less cooling power
Lower electricity costs
More reliable servers
Lower carbon emissions
Green Computing Techniques
05
Notes: Green techniques: intelligent cooling, temperature-based workload allocation, better hot-aisle and cold-aisle separation, and avoiding unnecessary cooling or fan use. Example: when one rack gets too hot, workloads shift to cooler servers. Benefits: reduced cooling power, lower electricity costs, improved server reliability and reduced carbon emissions.

TECHNIQUE 03
Renewable-Aware Workload Management
Schedules computing tasks according to the availability of renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind power.
HOW IT WORKS
01
Energy monitoring
Tracks renewable energy generation and electricity demand.
02
Renewable forecasting
Predicts solar or wind energy availability.
03
Workload scheduling
Runs flexible, non-urgent tasks when renewable energy is abundant.
04
Grid coordination
Reduces reliance on carbon-intensive grid electricity where possible.
Green Computing Techniques
06
Notes: Renewable-aware workload management times computing tasks to match renewable energy availability. It monitors generation and demand, forecasts solar and wind output, runs flexible tasks when clean energy is plentiful, and reduces reliance on carbon-intensive grid power.

TECHNIQUE 03 · IN PRACTICE
Run flexible work when clean energy is plentiful
GREEN COMPUTING TECHNIQUES
Schedule batch processing during high solar generation.
Shift flexible workloads across time or locations.
Prioritize renewable-powered servers when practical.
Combine renewable forecasts with workload requirements.
EXAMPLE · COLLEGE DATA CENTER
Student-project model training is scheduled for the afternoon, when rooftop solar power generation is high.
BENEFITS
More renewable use
Lower carbon footprint
Lower costs*
Sustainable computing
Green Computing Techniques
07
*Where electricity tariffs permit
Notes: Green techniques: schedule batch jobs during high solar output, shift flexible workloads across time or locations, prefer renewable-powered servers, and combine energy forecasts with workload needs. Example: a college data center runs student model training in the afternoon when rooftop solar peaks. Benefits: more renewable energy use, lower carbon footprint, lower electricity costs where tariffs permit, and more sustainable computing.

SIDE BY SIDE
Comparing the Three Techniques
TECHNIQUE | MAIN FOCUS | PRIMARY GREEN BENEFIT
Edge–cloud collaborative computing | Where data is processed | Reduces unnecessary data transfer and computing
Thermal-aware data center optimization | Server temperature and cooling | Reduces cooling energy
Renewable-aware workload management | When and where tasks run, based on clean energy | Reduces carbon emissions
Green Computing Techniques
08
Notes: Each technique targets a different lever. Edge–cloud computing decides where data is processed and cuts unnecessary transfer and computing. Thermal-aware optimization focuses on temperature and cooling and cuts cooling energy. Renewable-aware management decides when and where tasks run based on clean energy and cuts carbon emissions.
